meta.title: Who really said "Those who dance are considered insane by those who cannot hear the music"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: George Carlin printed it in Brain Droppings (1997) but credited 'Anon.' It is an anonymous proverb; The Times called it old in 1927. Not Nietzsche.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Those who dance are considered insane by those who cannot hear the music'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Carlin, not Nietzsche. An anonymous proverb: The Times called it old in 1927, and the image goes back to Germaine de Stael in 1813.

answer.label: Not George Carlin — an old anonymous proverb
answer.authorDates: In print as an “old proverb” by 1927 · earliest recorded figure 1813
answer.sourceLine: The line has no known author. The Times of London printed a version in 1927 already labelled an “old proverb,” and the earliest recorded appearance of the image is Germaine de Staël’s On Germany (1813). Carlin did print this modern wording — page 74 of Brain Droppings (1997) — but when he used it again in 2001 he credited it to “Anon.”

source.heading: Where the line actually shows up

docMeta.dd: George Carlin; Hyperion, New York, 1997 — the line on page 74, credited to “Anon.” when reused in 2001
“They who dance are thought mad by those who hear not the music” — The Times (London), 1927, printed as an old proverb
Germaine de Staël, On Germany (1813), per Wikiquote

source.excerpt: They who dance are thought mad by those who hear not the music. The truth of the old proverb was never more surely borne out that [sic] it is just now.
trail: 1813 — Germaine de Staël, imagining a ball with the music inaudible, writes that “the dancing that we saw there would appear insane.” Wikiquote gives this as the first recorded appearance ↗.

1927 — The Times of London prints “They who dance are thought mad by those who hear not the music” and calls it an old proverb; a proverb dictionary picks up that instance in 1929 without finding anything earlier. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.

1997 — the modern wording appears on page 74 of George Carlin’s Brain Droppings; in Napalm & Silly Putty (2001) he prints it again and credits “Anon.” GeorgeCarlin.net, the long-running unofficial Carlin catalogue, documents both ↗.
Meanwhile — the saying is handed to Friedrich Nietzsche across the web, an attribution Wikiquote lists as misattributed ↗ and that no researcher has been able to substantiate.
source.excerptNote: This is the 1927 printing in The Times of London (16 February 1927) as transcribed by Quote Investigator — reproduced exactly, including the “borne out that it is” wording of the original, hence the [sic]. Seventy years before Brain Droppings, and already introduced as an old proverb rather than anyone’s coinage.

source.rightsNote: The sentence has no identifiable author — it was already being called an “old proverb” when The Times printed a version in 1927 — so quotle.info asserts no rights status for the saying itself and makes no public-domain claim. Note separately that the exact modern wording as it sits on page 74 of Brain Droppings (Hyperion, 1997) appears inside a book that is still in copyright, even though Carlin credited the line itself to “Anon.”

author.name: George Carlin
author.heading: Why Carlin’s name got attached
author.metaLine: 1937–2008 · American comedian, social critic and author
author.bio: George Carlin was an American stand-up comedian, satirist and author whose routines took apart politics, religion and above all the English language. He really did print this sentence — it sits on page 74 of his 1997 bestseller Brain Droppings, a grab-bag of jokes, lists and stray observations — but he was not claiming it: when the same line turned up in Napalm & Silly Putty (2001) it carried the credit “Anon.” Carlin is one of the internet’s most-forged names, and he said so himself in his 2001 essay “Don’t Blame Me,” posted on his own site georgecarlin.com: “Nothing you see on the Internet is mine unless it came from one of my albums, books, HBO shows, or appeared on my website.” The essay came down when that site was revamped in 2012, but the wording is preserved on the unofficial GeorgeCarlin.net ↗.

misattribution.heading: Three names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most heavily re-signed sentences on the internet. Every credit it carries has been checked and none of them holds.

items.why: By far the commonest credit, usually in the longer shape “And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music.” Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗, noting several pre-Nietzsche examples and the 1927 “old proverb” label; Quote Investigator states plainly that it “has not yet located substantive evidence that Nietzsche wrote or said the statement” ↗.

GeorgeCarlin.net, the long-running unofficial Carlin catalogue, puts it on its bogus-quotes list: “George Carlin quoted this line, but he didn’t compose it” ↗. It is on page 74 of Brain Droppings (1997), and when it reappeared in Napalm & Silly Putty (2001) he credited “Anon.”

items.tag: A poet no one can find
items.why: A widely copied variant — “Those who danced were thought to be quite insane by those who could not hear the music” — is credited to a poet of this name in a 2002 newspaper instance recorded by Quote Investigator ↗, which reports no evidence that such a poet exists.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no author to find. The saying was already old when The Times printed it in 1927 ↗, and its earliest recorded appearance is Germaine de Staël’s On Germany, 1813 ↗.

context.heading: A proverb that keeps getting adopted
lead: This sentence is a near-perfect specimen of how attribution drifts. It began as an observation rather than an epigram: Germaine de Staël, describing a moment of dissociation, imagined watching a ballroom with the music switched off — “the dancing that we saw there would appear insane.” Over the nineteenth century the image hardened into a saying, and by 1927 The Times of London could print it and call it old without feeling any need to say whose it was.

What happened next is the modern part of the story. A saying with no owner is unstable: every generation hands it to whoever it sounds like. It got pinned on Friedrich Nietzsche, who loved dancing as a metaphor but whom no researcher has been able to connect to this sentence; on a poet called “Angela Monet,” who cannot be found; and on George Carlin, who actually printed it — and then, four years later, honestly labelled it “Anon.”
context.detailsSummary: Why “he printed it” is not “he wrote it”
detailsBody: Brain Droppings is a collection of jokes, notions, lists and stray lines, and the unofficial GeorgeCarlin.net catalogue suggests the most likely explanation is the ordinary kind: he encountered a good line somewhere, it lodged, and it came back out later without its source attached. The correction is his own — the 2001 credit to “Anon.” is Carlin declining the authorship the internet later insisted on giving him.

The Nietzsche version circulates in a longer, more literary shape — “And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music” — which is not the wording Carlin printed and not a sentence traceable to Nietzsche’s books either.
context.pull: The proverb was already old in 1927. Everyone since has just been signing it.
